Empirical Research Plan: “Islamist Mayors and Women’s Empowerment in Turkey”

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Close-election Regression-Discontinuity Design (RD), supplemented by an RD-in-Differences (RDD-DiD) when a pre-treatment measure is available (e.g., 1990 vs. 2000 Censuses).

Why RD?  
• Mayoral control in 1994 is determined by first-past-the-post vote totals.  
• Within a narrow window around a zero vote-margin, assignment of an Islamic mayor (Refah) is as-good-as-random.  
• Outcomes are measured six years later (2000 Census) and in the long run (2011 ABPRS, later elections), so post-treatment periods are well defined.  
• Data richness allows all standard RD diagnostics and robustness tests.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if municipality’s 1994 mayoral election was won by the Refah (Islamic) Party.

Control group  
Municipalities in which Refah ran but narrowly lost in 1994 (vote-margin < 0). The “as-good-as-random” comparison is restricted to those within a data-driven bandwidth around the cutoff.

Treatment timing / event date  
Election date: 27 March 1994. Outcomes measured 1994-1999 (during tenure) and later.

Running variable and cutoff  
Running variable: Refah vote share – vote share of the runner-up (can be interpreted as Refah margin of victory).  
Cutoff: 0 (just lost vs. just won).

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff  
 No unobserved determinant of women’s outcomes jumps exactly at a zero vote-margin. Plausible because individual votes are too granular to be coordinated to achieve a specific margin.

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable  
 Ballot stuffing or recounts could in theory bias close elections; we will run a McCrary density test and inspect bunching. Turkey’s 1994 elections were monitored, making large-scale, margin-targeted fraud unlikely.

A3. Stable composition (SUTVA)  
 Treatment status of one municipality does not systematically alter women’s outcomes in another, except possibly in adjacent urban areas. We will check robustness excluding immediate neighbors and adding province × election-cycle fixed effects.

A4. First election drives treatment; later outcomes do not retro-determine it  
 All dependent variables are measured after the 1994 mayoral term begins, so reverse causality is ruled out.

A5. Continuity of covariates  
 Observable pre-1994 characteristics (from 1990 Census) must be smooth through the cutoff. We test this directly.

Overall, assumptions A1–A5 are plausible and empirically testable.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Vote-count manipulation or strategic candidate withdrawal  
 • McCrary density and sorting tests;  
 • Covariate balancing right vs. left of cutoff;  
 • Robustness to excluding elections decided by a recount or litigated result.

T2. Pre-existing trends in women’s empowerment (selection)  
 • RDD-DiD: use change between 1990 and 2000 Censuses as outcome; any pre-trend discontinuity would appear in 1990 data.  
 • Placebo tests with 1990 (pre-treatment) outcomes.

T3. Post-1994 political dynamics (e.g., Refah banned in 1998)  
 • Instrument subsequent Islamic mayoral control with 1994 win to estimate LATE of prolonged Islamist exposure.  
 • Control for province-time fixed effects and the fraction of council seats held by Islamists in 2004–2009 to net out later convergence.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# --- Load packages ----------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # regressions
library(rdrobust)    # RD estimation
library(ggplot2)

# --- 1. Data loading ----------
elec  <- fread("election_1994.csv")      # vote shares by municipality
cens00<- fread("census_2000.csv")        # post outcomes
cens90<- fread("census_1990.csv")        # pre outcomes
long  <- fread("longrun_2011.csv")       # ABPRS + later votes

# --- 2. Merge & construct variables ----------
dat <- merge(elec, cens00, by="muni_id")
dat <- merge(dat, cens90[,.(muni_id, female_hs_90 = female_hs_rate)], by="muni_id")
dat <- merge(dat, long, by="muni_id", all.x=TRUE)

# Running variable: Refah share minus runner-up
dat[, margin := refah_share - second_share]

# Treatment indicator
dat[, treat := as.integer(margin > 0)]

# Main outcomes (examples)
dat[, female_hs_00  := female_hs_rate]            # 2000 female high-school completion
dat[, teen_marriage := married_15_19_2011]        # 2011 teen marriage share
dat[, isl_vote_09   := isl_vote_share_2009]       # Islamic bloc vote share in 2009

# --- 3. RD bandwidth (Imbens-Kalyanaraman) ----------
bw <- IKbandwidth(dat$margin, dat$female_hs_00)

# --- 4. Main RD specification ----------
rd_main <- rdrobust(y = dat$female_hs_00,
                    x = dat$margin,
                    c = 0,
                    h = bw)

summary(rd_main)

# --- 5. RD-in-Differences robustness ----------
dat[, delta_hs := female_hs_00 - female_hs_90]

rd_diff <- rdrobust(y = dat$delta_hs,
                    x = dat$margin,
                    c = 0,
                    h = bw)
summary(rd_diff)

# --- 6. Covariate continuity check ----------
pre_covs <- c("log_pop_90", "urban_rate_90", "fem_lit_90")

for (v in pre_covs){
  print(
    rdrobust(y = dat[[v]], x = dat$margin, c = 0, h = bw)$coef[1:2]
  )
}

# --- 7. Graphical RD plot ----------
rdplot(dat$female_hs_00, dat$margin, c=0, binselect="esmv")
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Direction  
• Female empowerment outcomes (secular high-school completion, age at marriage) likely decline when Refah controls the municipality.  
• Female political participation in Islamist structures (e.g., voting for Islamic parties) likely rises.

Magnitude (ballpark)  
• −2 to −4 percentage-point effect on girls’ high-school completion (baseline ≈ 30 %).  
• +1 to +2 pp on marriage rates for 15-19 girls (baseline ≈ 10 %).  
• +3 pp in subsequent Islamic vote share (baseline ≈ 20 %).

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RD)
------------------------------------------------------------
C1. No manipulation of the running variable ………………… 1  
C2. Covariates smooth at cutoff ……………………………… 1  
C3. Correct functional form & bandwidth choice ………… 1  
C4. No interference/spillovers across units ………………… 0  
C5. Outcome measured after treatment, no attrition ……… 1  

Overall score: 4 / 5.
